title: Square Root and Cube Root Functions

blocks.html: The square root and cube root are two of the Parent Functions, and you transform them with the same moves as any other parent. What makes them special is where they start (square root) and where they are centered (cube root). You will use nth Roots to read their domains.

$f(x) = a\sqrt{x - h} + k$ starts at the point $(h, k)$; its domain is $[h, \infty)$ and its range is $[k, \infty)$ if $a > 0$ or $(-\infty, k]$ if $a < 0$. $g(x) = a\sqrt[3]{x - h} + k$ has domain and range all real numbers and is symmetric about its center $(h, k)$.

A square root needs a nonnegative input, so the graph starts exactly where the inside is 0 and goes one way from there. Its outputs start at 0 and grow, so after stretching by $a$ and shifting by $k$ they start at $k$ and go up (or down, if $a < 0$). A cube root accepts every input and gives every output, so its graph runs across the whole plane.

blocks.title: Domain, range and starting point
steps: Inside $x + 3 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -3$: domain $[-3, \infty)$. The graph starts at $(-3, 4)$.
$\sqrt{x + 3} \ge 0$, and multiplying by $-2$ makes it $\le 0$; adding 4 gives $f(x) \le 4$.
blocks.a: Starts at $(-3, 4)$, goes down and to the right; domain $[-3, \infty)$, range $(-\infty, 4]$.

blocks.title: A cube root
steps: Shift $\sqrt[3]{x}$ right 1 and up 2. Its center moves from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 2)$.
Cube roots accept all inputs, so the domain and range are all real numbers.

blocks.html: Giving a cube root function a restricted domain, as if it were a square root. $\sqrt[3]{x - 1}$ is defined for every $x$, including $x = -7$, where it equals $-2$. Only even roots require a nonnegative inside.
